body.heading: The method: split, guess, multiply
paragraphs: The physicist Enrico Fermi was famous for answering absurd questions - how many piano tuners are in Chicago? - with nothing but reasoning. His method has three moves. Break the impossible question into small questions you can estimate. Round your guesses boldly; precision is not the point. Then multiply the chain together, trusting that your overestimates and underestimates will partly cancel.

The surprising thing is how well it works. A Fermi estimate usually lands within a factor of ten of the truth, and often much closer - close enough to make decisions, check headlines, and detect nonsense. It is the mathematics of 'roughly right on purpose'.

body.heading: The piano tuners, worked
paragraphs: Here is the classic, with Fermi-style round numbers. Chicago's population: about 3 million. Average household: about 3 people, so roughly 1 million households. Fraction owning a piano: guess 1 in 20, giving about 50,000 pianos. Pianos need tuning about once a year, so the city needs roughly 50,000 tunings annually.

Now the tuner's side: say a tuner manages about 4 tunings a day and works about 250 days a year - roughly 1,000 tunings a year. Divide 50,000 by 1,000 and you get about 50 piano tuners. Historical checks against city directories put the true figure in the dozens - the chain of guesses landed. Every link was crude; the answer was not.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Try Fermi's favourite party piece: estimate the number of heartbeats in your lifetime. A resting heart beats about 70 times a minute. Multiply by 60 minutes, 24 hours, 365 days and 80 years and you land near 3 billion beats - a number worth pausing on.

Then set your own question: how many litres of water does your school or workplace drink in a year? How many slices of pizza does your town eat on a Friday? State every assumption out loud as you go - the assumptions are the method, and arguing about them is where the learning lives.

takeaway: Big questions become answerable when you split them into small guesses and multiply - being roughly right on purpose beats being precisely stuck.
